reports.name: Pete Crow-Armstrong
reports.published_report: The xwOBA (.358) and hard-hit rate (48.5%) say there's a plus power-speed bat here, and the 11.8% walk rate confirms he earns his way on base when pitchers work around him. The problem sitting in the middle of this profile is a 26.9% strikeout rate: the gap between a .250 xBA and a .464 xSLG tells you the contact is noisy, that he's generating loft and impact on a subset of swings while the 33.9% chase rate costs him on the rest. If he can hold that walk rate and take a step toward tightening the zone, the projection's .877 OPS across 710 PA with 34 home runs and 38 stolen bases is the kind of five-category season that defines a lineup. Doesn't tighten the chase, and you're looking at a volatile middle-of-the-order piece who runs and mashes but goes cold in predictable stretches.

reports.name: Shohei Ohtani
reports.published_report: The Statcast batting profile is almost uniformly elite, .405 xwOBA, 93.4 mph average exit velocity, 16.5% barrel rate, and then you hit the 30.8% whiff rate sitting in the 15th percentile, a real crack in an otherwise immaculate picture. The contact quality says true middle-of-the-order force; the swing-and-miss says he still gives away at-bats, and a projection of .286/.388/.547 with 37 home runs in 688 plate appearances is what you get when those two things coexist. On the mound, the 2.72 xERA and 27.9% strikeout rate describe a genuine front-of-rotation arm, and the 3.8% barrel rate against him tells you hitters aren't squaring him up even when they make contact. The whole profile hinges on staying healthy enough to do both things across a full Dodger season, because there's no adjusted version of this player, only Ohtani at full strength, or a dramatically smaller read.

reports.name: Bobby Witt Jr.
reports.published_report: The xBA sitting at .299 is the loudest number in a profile full of loud numbers, and it explains why a .285 projection feels conservative rather than generous. Witt makes hard contact at a 51.5% hard-hit rate with a 92.6 mph average exit velocity, and he does it fast enough that 30.2 ft/s sprint speed turns singles into doubles and grounders into infield hits the way most shortstops can't. The one real tension in the profile is a 33.5% chase rate that keeps the bat-to-ball gains from fully cashing, though a 17.6% strikeout rate suggests he still squares enough of that contact to escape the worst consequences. If the chase rate tightens even modestly, the .378 xwOBA stops looking like a ceiling and starts looking like a floor.

What makes it credible is the shape: his 22.0% strikeout rate is roughly league-average, his walk rate clocks at 10.0%, and he barrels the ball at an elite clip without relying on an elite hard-hit rate, which means the damage is concentrated rather than volume-dependent. At 22 with that power-to-contact balance, projecting to 33 home runs and a .811 OPS isn't a leap. The whole thing hinges on whether the xBA sitting at .250 is a batted-ball profile issue or a real hit-tool ceiling, because if the average settles below the projected .260, the offensive value narrows considerably, but the power floor stays.

reports.name: James Wood
reports.published_report: The contact risk is documented and it isn't shrinking — 28.6% strikeouts, a whiff rate in the 16th percentile, and none of that is going away. What makes Wood so hard to dismiss is that the contact he does make is essentially maxed out: 95.1 mph average exit velocity at the 100th percentile, a 20.8% barrel rate also at the 100th, and an xSLG of .585 that describes a hitter who does catastrophic damage when he connects. Layer in a 16.8% walk rate that almost no hitters in the league match, and the .419 xwOBA tells you the strikeouts are a tax, not a ceiling. If it holds, you get something close to the projected .264/.388/.526 line with 36 home runs across 656 plate appearances; if the strikeout rate climbs further, the walks and raw power are still enough to carry a plus offensive profile.

reports.name: CJ Abrams
reports.published_report: The .862 OPS projection is built on a Statcast profile that's more interesting than its raw numbers suggest. His xwOBA sits at .345 and his xSLG at .450, both grading well into the upper half of the league, and a 10.2% barrel rate that outpaces what his 89.6 mph average exit velocity would typically produce tells you the quality contact is landing on the right swings. The 37.2% chase rate is the structural problem, sitting at just the 13th percentile, and the 29.2% whiff rate means zone expansion doesn't just hurt the walk total, it converts directly into strikeouts. His 28.5 ft/s sprint speed gives this profile a second dimension, 31 projected steals buying him value that survives a rough offensive stretch, but the gap between the everyday shortstop this line describes and a streaky, platoon-adjacent version closes almost entirely on whether that chase behavior improves.

reports.name: Jackson Merrill
reports.published_report: The xSLG sits at .467 and the hard-hit rate at 47.3%, and those two numbers tell you what kind of player he actually is: a young outfielder who contacts the ball hard enough that the power grade is legitimate regardless of what a .246 projection average suggests. The chase rate at 36.8% is the real friction point, because a hitter who expands the zone that aggressively and walks only 6.3% of the time is going to bleed batting average and OBP against good stuff, and the projection's .297 OBP reflects exactly that cost. What saves the profile is 29.0 ft/s sprint speed and 25 projected home runs alongside 28 steals, a combination that produces genuine fantasy value and an everyday role even when the hit tool runs cold. If the chase rate ever tightens, the .467 xSLG says the offensive ceiling jumps considerably; if it doesn't, he's a 25/28 corner bat with a soft OBP who needs lineup protection to stay valuable.

Juneiker Caceres has walked and struck out exactly 36 times apiece across A+ & A this season, a 12/12 BB%/K% split that translates to a K-rate below league average and a BB-rate just above it at the MLB equivalent level. The .311/.409/.516 across 291 plate appearances is loud on its face, and a .324 BABIP keeps it honest enough that the shape isn't doing all the heavy lifting. The ceiling here is a bench or platoon bat, and it gets there only if the plus contact rates hold as the stuff gets sharper in the upper levels, because the ISO translates to .135 at the MLB equivalent level, well shy of average power, and without the bat-to-ball skill carrying its weight this becomes an org depth outcome in a hurry.

reports.name: Ezequiel Duran
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile is quietly below average almost everywhere that matters for a hitter. His xwOBA sits at .302, his hard-hit rate is 36.2%, and a 35.9% chase rate explains why the contact isn't translating even when it's made. What keeps the projection at .261/.314/.425 with 16 home runs is the one genuine weapon: 29.0 ft/s sprint speed that grades at the 89th percentile, buying him hits on the ground and keeping the stolen base total (12) credible. The whole profile hinges on whether that speed continues to prop up a batting average his expected numbers don't really support, because if the legs fade or the chase rate climbs further, what's left is a second-division regular with a thin offensive floor.

reports.name: Héctor Rodríguez
reports.published_report: The .259 ISO at AAA is loud for a 22-year-old, and the translation says it carries: an MLB-equivalent ISO of .190 against a big-league context where .150 is the baseline. The discipline profile is the honest constraint — 42 walks against 93 strikeouts in 455 AAA plate appearances translates to a walk rate and a strikeout rate that both land right at MLB average, which means the bat has to carry him with no margin for a power regression. If the raw over-the-fence ability holds at the big-league level, Héctor Rodríguez is a real bench bat who can be deployed against righties; if the power thins out in translation, the walk rate won't save the profile.

reports.name: Dillon Dingler
reports.published_report: Thirty-two home runs from a catcher with a .360 xwOBA is a profile that doesn't need much salesmanship. What makes Dingler's Statcast card interesting is the disconnect between his 88.9 mph average exit velocity, which sits below the middle of the league, and an .493 xSLG that suggests he's finding the barrel at the right moments rather than just hitting the ball hard across the board. The 33.9% chase rate is a real drag on his 6.0% walk rate, and if pitchers learn to work him soft and away, the power production becomes more dependent on pitch selection he hasn't yet shown. At full health and 628 projected plate appearances, this is a middle-of-the-order catcher, not a platoon piece.

reports.name: Nick Gonzales
reports.published_report: The xBA sits at .281 while exit velocity and barrel rate are both bottom-decile, and that gap is the whole profile. Gonzales makes enough contact, and makes it to the right parts of the field often enough, that batted-ball quality barely matters — his 16.9% strikeout rate keeps him in counts and his legs (28.8 ft/s sprint speed) turn soft contact into something usable. The projection's .299 AVG with a .353 OBP across 630 PA is believable precisely because it doesn't ask the power to show up: 8 home runs is the honest ceiling, not a floor being sandbagged. Everything hinges on the hit tool holding at a league-above clip, because if the contact quality regresses toward what the 86.2 mph average exit velocity implies, there's a below-average walk rate and no thump to fall back on.

reports.name: Cam Caminiti
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the argument. If the command develops, there's a back-end starter here; if it doesn't, he's a depth arm.

reports.name: A.J. Ewing
reports.published_report: The legs are the loudest thing on this card. At 29.5 ft/s, Ewing's sprint speed sits at the 95th percentile, and the projection trusts it enough to hand him 23 projected steals across 479 plate appearances. The contact profile is the tension: a 25.4% strikeout rate that grades in the 23rd percentile drags against a 26.5% chase rate that's actually above average, meaning the whiffs come more from swing-and-miss than from expanding the zone, which is at least the more fixable version of the problem. The Statcast contact quality is quietly decent, with an xBA of .259 and hard-hit rate of 43.9%, so if he tightens the zone even modestly he fits as a fringe everyday outfielder; if the strikeouts persist at this volume, he's a speed-first bench piece whose .704 OPS projection already has that ceiling baked in.

reports.name: Ryan Weathers
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile is a puzzle that doesn't fully resolve. Weathers misses bats at a 27.3% whiff rate and keeps his walk rate at 7.0%, both sitting comfortably above the median, but when contact happens it's hard contact — 41.8% hard-hit rate, a barrel rate at 8.4%, and an xERA of 4.26 that reflects real damage done when hitters square him up. The strikeout and walk numbers say the stuff plays; the contact profile says the margin for error is thin when he misses in the zone rather than out of it. His 3.66 ERA projection across 155.3 innings lives between those two realities, asking you to believe the discipline metrics carry more weight than the exit velocity profile does. That's a reasonable bet, not a lock.

reports.name: Caleb Durbin
reports.published_report: The Statcast contact profile is almost entirely a warning: 83.8 mph average exit velocity and a 26.4% hard-hit rate are both deep in the bottom handful of qualified hitters, and the .326 xSLG says the 15 projected home runs are being carried by the projection's playing-time assumption more than by what he's actually doing to the ball. What keeps this from being a simple cut is a 13.7% strikeout rate that barely touches average, a whiff rate sitting at 15.7%, and enough defensive value at the hot corner to make him a real roster asset. If the speed (19 projected steals) and contact control hold and the exit velocity ticks up even modestly, he profiles as a low-end everyday third baseman who earns his lineup spot through discipline and legs rather than thump. If the soft contact is the permanent version of him, you're looking at a useful bench piece with a good glove and not much else.

reports.name: Henry Bolte
reports.published_report: The sprint speed carries this profile and the contact is what threatens it. Bolte runs 30.6 ft/s, a perfect 100th-percentile mark, and a 47.5% hard-hit rate shows he punishes mistakes when he finds them. But a 33.2% whiff rate bleeds into a .304 xwOBA, and the projection's .258/.329/.379 line reflects a hitter whose bat-to-ball issues are already eating the raw pop. Everything hinges on whether he can close the gap between how hard he hits the ball and how often he actually hits it, because if the whiff rate stays where it is, he's a fourth outfielder running himself into lineup spots rather than earning them.

reports.name: Cam Smith
reports.published_report: The 11.6% barrel rate and 45.1% hard-hit rate are legitimately above average contact quality, but the 28.7% whiff rate is eating the return on that power. The Statcast gap between his .435 xSLG and a projected .398 SLG tells the story of a hitter whose best swings produce real damage, while the contact consistency (.246 xBA) drags the overall line toward .225 projected average and a .694 OPS across a full season. Add 29.3 ft/s sprint speed that ranks at the 93rd percentile and a 91st-percentile fielding profile, and you have a profile that carries its weight everywhere except the zone. If he tightens the whiff rate, the power plays up and he becomes a solid regular; if he doesn't, 20 home runs and plus defense make him a serviceable outfielder who needs lineup protection to stay in the middle of a card.

reports.name: MacKenzie Gore
reports.published_report: The contact quality numbers are the tension in this profile. An 8.8% barrel rate and 42.0% hard-hit rate, both in the bottom quarter of the league, suggest Gore is getting hit harder than his strikeout rate implies, and the xERA of 3.84 sits roughly a half-run better than the 4.28 projection precisely because the projection factors in the contact risk the Statcast surface is revealing. The 25.8 K% is genuine production, but the 8.5 BB% keeps the profile from being elite, and the whiff and chase numbers are solidly above-average without being dominant. What he actually is: a volume innings starter who misses bats at a useful rate, keeps the ball in the yard often enough, but gets tagged when contact happens, and if the walk rate climbs, the ERA follows while the gap between xERA and projection closes in the wrong direction.

The .219 ISO and 18 home runs in 428 plate appearances are loud, and the translated ISO of .158 lands close enough to the MLB average that the power travels, if modestly. What keeps this from being a cleaner story is the walk rate: 11% at the level translates to 9.4%, which is fine but not the amplifier the surface OBP implies. The profile hinges entirely on whether the contact and raw power hold at the catcher position as pitching quality rises — if both do, this becomes a genuine everyday catcher; if the bat thins out at AAA, you're left with a serviceable backup who can hit.

reports.name: Trevor Rogers
reports.published_report: The gap between a 33.9% chase rate and a 20.3% strikeout rate is the whole argument here. Hitters expand, then foul things off or make contact anyway, because a 23.3% whiff rate doesn't give him the weapon to finish them. The control is real enough, 6.8% walks, and a 3.89 xERA suggests he's pitching closer to average than a 4.22 ERA projection implies. Whether he closes that gap depends entirely on finding a swing-and-miss offering to match the chase; without it, he's a back-of-rotation arm who eats innings and collects quality starts without accumulating much else.

reports.name: Termarr Johnson
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the loudest thing in this profile, and also the most complicated. At AAA in 2026, Termarr Johnson has drawn 68 walks against 101 strikeouts across 406 plate appearances, and that 17% walk rate translates to 13.1% at the MLB level, where most hitters sit around 8.5%. The power, though, is a different story: his .120 ISO at AAA translates to .114 in the majors, well short of the .150 MLB average, and a .199 average sitting on a .259 BABIP suggests the contact isn't beating defenders when it lands. The 24 stolen bases at AAA matter here, because if the legs can manufacture value that the bat isn't yet providing, the floor stays livable, but everything hinges on whether the contact quality catches up enough to make opposing pitchers respect the plate discipline instead of just pitching around it. Right now the ceiling is a bench or platoon bat, and the floor is the same.

reports.published_report: The 1.60 ERA across AA & A+ is the loudest number in the system right now, but the translation is where Eyanson's profile gets more honest. That gap between the raw 12.6 K/9 and 0.90 WHIP at the minor-league level and what carries over tells you the command is functional but not a weapon, and the 27% K-BB% across AA & A+ sits at the 98th percentile in the pitcher pool with 110 strikeouts in 78.6 innings backing the shape of it. reports.name: Garrett Mitchell

He doesn't chase (22.8%), draws walks at 12.3%, and runs at 29.9 feet per second, so the floor is legitimate: a projection of .246/.343/.397 with 16 steals is a useful outfielder. reports.name: Michael King
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile is a paradox, and ValuCast's 3.56 ERA projection is betting on the resolution. King's hard-hit rate sits at 32.4%, well below the field, and his average exit velocity of 87.3 mph reflects genuinely suppressed contact, but his xERA is 4.38 and his K% at 21.2% is ordinary, which means the soft contact isn't coming from missing bats. The walk rate at 9.6% is the problem holding the profile together wrong: he's not getting enough swings-and-misses to carry that free-pass volume, and until that tightens, the xwOBA at .322 is the more honest ledger than the ERA projection implies. If the command holds at something closer to his contact-suppression quality, he's a functional mid-rotation starter eating 184 innings; if the walks stay where they are and the weak contact regresses even a little, he's a back-end arm whose ERA drifts toward what the underlying metrics already say.

reports.name: Corey Seager
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile has two faces that don't fully reconcile. A 15.4% barrel rate and a .456 xSLG say there's genuine thump when he connects, and a 12.4% walk rate keeps him on base enough to matter. But a 34.5% whiff rate is doing real damage to what those barrels could produce, and the projection's .222 AVG reflects that the contact quality doesn't translate into hits at the rate the power metrics imply. If the whiff rate softens even modestly, you get something closer to that .456 xSLG expressing itself in a full line; if it doesn't, 418 projected plate appearances at .735 OPS is a well-paid shortstop coasting on walks and home run upside he can't fully cash.

What it doesn't carry is power, with an ISO of .127 across A+ & A that translates to .104 at the MLB level while the MLB average sits at .150, and 22 stolen bases suggest he knows it. reports.published_report: The contact is elite and the power is essentially absent. Kasevich's 11% strikeout rate at AAA translates to 14.8% in MLB context, roughly half of what most major-league hitters post, and his 48 walks in 479 plate appearances have built a .376 OBP that does genuine work. The problem is that .376 gets there almost entirely without thump: four home runs in a full AAA season, an ISO that translates to .096, a profile that wins by not missing rather than by doing damage. If the hit tool and discipline carry over and he holds shortstop, he's a useful bench piece; if the glove slips or a roster decides the light bat isn't worth carrying, there's not much left to argue with.

reports.name: Luis Peña
reports.published_report:
The .299 average at A+ is the loud number, but the .376 BABIP is what you have to sit with. At 19, with 27 stolen bases in 214 plate appearances, the speed is doing obvious work, and a .383 OBP backed by 23 walks shows enough feel for the zone to take seriously. The problem is the power: .125 ISO at A+ translates to .116 in MLB-equivalent terms, well short of a league-average mark, and nothing in this profile suggests that gap closes.

reports.name: Andry Lara
reports.published_report: The K/9 at AAA is 7.3, and when you translate that to a major-league context it barely moves — 7.2, while MLB pitchers average 8.6. That gap is the whole problem. Lara has walked 36 and struck out 76 across 93.7 innings at AAA, and the walk rate translates almost identically to what big-league pitchers run while the strikeout rate sits well below it, leaving a translated K-BB% of 9.8% where the MLB average is 13.5%. The 5.60 ERA and 1.4 WHIP at AAA are effects, not the cause; a pitcher who can't miss bats at this level has very little margin for anything going wrong when the contact quality improves. If there's a developmental leap in stuff or command that hasn't shown up in these 93.7 innings, the floor scenario and the ceiling scenario collapse into the same thing: an organizational depth arm.
